opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting parts of what we're building. Most people's mental model of an AI assistant is still very transactional: you ask a question, you get an answer, and that answer is a snapshot of the web at that moment. But a lot of what we actually care about isn't static. You want to know when a product you've been eyeing drops in price, when a new paper comes out in your niche, when a policy changes, when tickets open up for something. The answer to "what's going on with X?" today is different from the answer next Tuesday.

So when a scout runs the same query over and over, the interesting problem shifts from "find the answer" to "figure out what's *new* and what actually *matters* to this person." That's surprisingly subtle. The web is noisy. Pages get re-dated, articles get republished, the same news gets syndicated across a dozen sites. A naive system would ping you constantly with things that look new but aren't. So the agent has to keep a kind of memory of what it has already seen and what it has already told you, and reason about whether something is a genuine change or just churn.

Then there's the question of judgment. If I've asked a scout to track, say, developments in a particular research area, not every new paper deserves a notification. Over time you want the scout to learn what crosses the bar for me specifically, so it's less like a keyword alert and more like a thoughtful colleague who says, "Hey, you'll probably want to see this."

And from a research perspective, it's a really nice setting because you get repeated interactions on the same intent. You can watch how the world evolves, see how well the agent tracks it, and get feedback on whether its updates were useful. That loop of persistent intent, changing information, and evolving understanding of the user is, to me, where a lot of the real value of agents on the web is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response describes remembering prior results to filter duplicates and detect genuine changes, but does not identify reusing prior work across repeated executions as an opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find fascinating is that the web isn't a static document, it's a living system, and a scout query is essentially a probe you drop into that system over and over. The first time you run it, you get a snapshot. But the interesting signal is in the deltas. When I ask the same question week after week, I'm not really asking "what's true right now," I'm asking "what's changing, and why?"

A few things jump out at me. One is that the shape of what comes back tells you about the information ecosystem itself. If a topic goes from a handful of primary sources to dozens of derivative pieces, you can watch an idea propagate, get distorted, get summarized, get re-summarized. You can see when consensus forms and when it fractures. That's not something you observe from a single query, no matter how good the retrieval is.

The second thing is that it exposes how brittle a lot of our assumptions about "answers" are. We tend to think of a question as having an answer, and the model's job is to find it. But for a huge class of questions, the honest answer is a trajectory. Prices, research results, who's working on what, what people believe about a technology. The repeated query turns the agent from an oracle into something more like a sensor, and I think that's a much more honest framing of what these systems can do.

And the third piece, which is the one I personally find most compelling, is the design question it raises. If the system is running the same scout on a schedule, when should it bother me? Most of the time nothing meaningful has changed, and surfacing noise erodes trust fast. So you end up having to think hard about what counts as a change worth knowing about, versus churn. That's a really interesting problem at the intersection of modeling, interface design, and understanding the user, and it's one where I think we've barely scratched the surface.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tracking changes between repeated scout queries, but does not identify redundant work across executions or suggest reusing prior work.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that the query can stay the same, but the answer can evolve. You’re expressing an interest once, and then, as new information becomes available, the scout can revisit that interest for you. That shifts the experience from having to remember to search for something to having something keep an eye on it for you.

And then the interesting challenge is deciding what’s worth bringing back. Has something meaningfully changed, or are we just seeing the same information in a different form? You want it to surface useful updates without creating more noise.

r001.rationale: The response notes that repeated searches may surface the same information and should distinguish meaningful updates from noise, but it does not identify that redundancy as an opportunity to reuse work.
